blocked.what: Closing the two defects found in RunState this period (PRO-0002, non-finite dt poisons ElapsedSeconds; PRO-0003, RegisterKill mutates Kills before it validates)
blocked.blockedOn: Both fixes are production code in Assets/Core/Run/RunState.cs, which this division may never write. They need a triage ruling and a work order to engineering. PRO-0002 additionally needs an authorised specification change before anyone touches the tests it invalidates, because two currently-passing assertions encode the defect and rewriting them without that authorisation is indistinguishable from weakening a test to go green.

notes:
RULING ON VERIFICATION ADEQUACY (WO-0007, Assets/Tests/Core.Tests/RunStateVerificationTests.cs). Adequate against the twelve criteria, and I confirm the specialist's finding of no criterion failure -- I re-derived it rather than accepted it, and I am filing no challenge. Every criterion is covered, coverage is traceable criterion by criterion, and the strongest work is on criterion 3: Criterion3_ZeroDtStillIncrements and EdgeCase_ZeroDtDoesNotCauseIssues genuinely discriminate a direct counter from one derived off ElapsedSeconds, which is the property criterion 3 was written to force, and would fail against a plausible wrong implementation. That is testing against the specification. But the green is thinner than it looks in three places and weaker than it looks in one, and I am recording all four so the gate's meaning is not overstated.

WHERE THE GREEN IS THIN. (1) Criterion 12 has no real test. Criterion12_TickTakesDtAsParameter merely calls Tick(1.0f) and asserts TickCount == 1; it says nothing whatever about UnityEngine, and a section header claiming otherwise is not coverage. This is nonetheless acceptable, because the criterion is enforced mechanically and better elsewhere: Studio/build/check-core-purity.sh greps Core sources for UnityEngine and UnityEditor with comments stripped, and asserts the asmdef still sets noEngineReferences. That is the real evidence and it runs at G2 without a licence. The test should not be mistaken for it. (2) Criterion 9 -- no wall-clock, static counter or unseeded source -- is not provable by a unit test at all. Constructing two RunStates and finding both equal DefaultSeed does refute a clock and a global counter, which is worth having, but the actual evidence is source inspection, and I did it: Seed is a get-only property assigned once from the constructor parameter, DefaultSeed is a const uint, and there is no other write path. (3) Criterion 1 says "every value representable by the seed's type" and the verification samples ten uints. Exhaustive coverage of 2^32 is not a reasonable ask; the sample includes 0, 1, uint.MaxValue and both sides of the int boundary, which is where a substitution or a signed round-trip would show. I accept it as written and note only that the criterion's wording promises more than any test delivers.

WHERE THE GREEN IS WEAKER THAN IT LOOKS, AND THIS ONE MATTERS. Criterion3_NaNDtIncrements and Criterion3_PositiveInfinityDtIncrements are the specialist drifting from testing the specification to confirming the implementation. The tell is in the test's own comment: "NaN comparison '< 0' is always false, so NaN passes the dt < 0 check". That is a description of the code reasoned forward into an assertion, not a requirement reasoned down from the criterion. Criterion 3 says a non-throwing Tick must increment regardless of dt; it does not say NaN must be non-throwing. The specialist inferred the premise from the implementation and then verified the implementation against it, which is circular, and it produced a passing test that certifies a defect as intended behaviour. Both tests assert only TickCount and never look at ElapsedSeconds, which is precisely where the damage lands. That is the shape of drift I want specialists to recognise: an edge case discovered by reading the guard, rather than derived from the contract, needs the contract consulted before it becomes an assertion.

WHAT I FOUND READING THE IMPLEMENTATION MYSELF. Two defects, neither covered by any of the twelve criteria, both filed as proposals rather than challenges because the implementation satisfies WO-0007 as written and the specification is what is short. First, PRO-0002: Tick's guard is `dt < 0f` while the exception message it throws states "dt must be >= 0." Those predicates differ on NaN, which satisfies neither, so NaN passes the guard and reaches `ElapsedSeconds += dt`. NaN is absorbing under addition, so one such call destroys the run clock permanently -- every later valid Tick leaves it NaN, only Reset recovers, no exception is raised, IsOver stays false and TickCount keeps counting correctly. Infinity saturates the same way. It is silent, and it defeats the seed-plus-tick coordinate WO-0007 exists to build, because the tick number reads as trustworthy while the clock beside it is not a number. Second, PRO-0003: RegisterKill increments Kills before delegating validation to AddScore, so RegisterKill(-1) leaves Kills incremented and then throws -- a method that mutates two fields is not atomic on its failure path, and the exception it surfaces names paramName "amount" rather than scoreValue, pointing a reporter at the wrong method. Assets/Unity/GameManager.cs:47 passes an unvalidated int straight through, and an exception thrown inside a Unity callback is logged and swallowed, so the inflated count survives to the reported score. No test in either suite calls RegisterKill with a negative value.

WHY NO CHALLENGE. I checked each finding against the twelve criteria before choosing the instrument. Criterion 4 obliges only dt < 0 to throw; NaN is not less than zero. Criterion 3 obliges any non-throwing Tick to increment, which the implementation does. Criterion 11 freezes the pre-existing contract, and both the dt guard and RegisterKill's ordering are pre-existing. So the implementer met the specification and a challenge against engineering would be unfounded. The gap is in the acceptance criteria, and PRO-0002 accordingly proposes a thirteenth criterion authored by the work-order author rather than a bare code change.

STANDING RULING ON THE GATE'S MEANING. G2 green on WO-0007 means the twelve criteria hold and Core stays engine-free. It does not mean RunState is free of defects, and this period demonstrates the difference: two real defects sit inside a fully green suite, one of them held in place by a passing assertion. I am not weakening or waiving anything, and I am marking nothing complete -- completed is empty, WO-0007 stays inFlight, and the G2 verdict is not mine to give. The narrower lesson for this division, which I will carry into the next verification brief: an acceptance criterion is a floor, and where a criterion's edge cases were derived by reading the implementation rather than the contract, that must be stated in the verification record instead of asserted as a requirement.

BOUNDARIES OBSERVED. I wrote no production code and no test code; Assets/** is untouched by me, including the tests I have criticised, and PRO-0002 deliberately hands the test rewrite to engineering under an explicit authorisation rather than performing it. I amended no acceptance criteria. needsFounderAttention is empty because nothing here is founder-only: both findings are triageable inside the studio, and no gate needs weakening to accommodate either.
